instructions:
You are an auditor checking one checklist item against the FDA web page paragraph it claims to come from. You get
the unit's paragraphs (reference and exact text of the page; "context" entries are headings) and the item. Start from the ITEM:
read it, then find in the cited paragraph what it covers.

The item must state one whole obligation of the cited paragraph. A condition, number, frequency or qualifier of
the same obligation left out of the item counts as omitted, including a condition in the lead-in above a list
item (the paragraph ending ":" above it). Judge only what
the statement's own words say: do not read the text back into the item. The condition field is a label, not part
of the statement: a condition or qualifier that appears only there is omitted from the statement.

Answer strictly:
- quote_as_printed: is the quote in the cited paragraph's text exactly (true/false)?
- verdict: "correct" only if the quote is exact, the paragraph expects what the statement asks for (an instruction
  to the investigator, "Determine whether the firm validated ...", expects the firm to have that practice), the statement
  adds nothing and omits nothing of that obligation, the strength (a legal requirement: shall/must/required = mandatory;
  should, FDA expects/recommends, an inspection point = recommended; may/acceptable = optional; a list item takes
  its lead-in's) matches, and the text applies to every listed plant
  type (INJ = sterile injectables: text limited to non-sterile products does not apply to
  INJ; text limited to sterile products applies only to INJ and API); otherwise "incorrect".
- reason: one or two sentences saying what you checked for THIS item, in this item's own words: name the
  condition, number, list or scope you compared with the text (e.g. "the 30-day limit and 'each lot' are both in
  the statement", "the list of components, containers and closures is complete", "drops the lead-in's 'for
  sterile products'"). Write each reason fresh for its item: a reason that would fit any item ("quote exact,
  strength matches, nothing added or omitted") or that repeats another answer's reason is not an answer, and the
  item then counts as unchecked.

Write the answers file named in your task: {"answers": [{"id", "verdict", "quote_as_printed", "reason"}, ...]}.

paragraphs.text: The most common problem associated with the production of these dosage forms is microbiological contamination caused by faulty design and/or control of purified water systems. During inspections, evaluate the adequacy of the water system. Review and evaluate the micro/chemistry test results on the routine monitoring of the water system including validation of the water system. Review any microbiological tests done on the finished drug including in-process testing.
paragraphs.heading_path: Dosage Form Drug Manufacturers cGMPs (10/93) > GUIDE TO INSPECTIONS OF DOSAGE FORM DRUG MANUFACTURER'S - CGMPR'S > II. CURRENT GOOD

paragraphs.text: Some of these drugs have preservatives added which protect them from microbial contamination. The preservatives are used primarily in multiple-dose containers to inhibit the growth of microorganisms introduced inadvertently during or after manufacturing. Evaluate the adequacy of preservative system. Preservative effectiveness testing for these products should be reviewed. For additional information, review the "Antimicrobial Preservatives-Effectiveness" section of the U.S.P..
paragraphs.heading_path: Dosage Form Drug Manufacturers cGMPs (10/93) > GUIDE TO INSPECTIONS OF DOSAGE FORM DRUG MANUFACTURER'S - CGMPR'S > II. CURRENT GOOD

paragraphs.text: Equipment employed for manufacturing topical drugs is sometimes difficult to clean. This is especially true for those which contain insoluble active ingredients, such as the sulfa drugs. The firm's equipment cleaning procedures including cleaning validation data should be reviewed and evaluated.

paragraphs.text: Packaging and labeling operations must be controlled so only those drugs which meet the specifications established in the master formula records are distributed. Review in detail the packaging and labeling operations to decide if the system will prevent drug and label mix-ups. Approximately 25% of all drug recalls originate in this area.
